promises.text: 2024 campaign: Said he would "Lower real estate taxes and eliminate wasteful spending."
2024 campaign: Said he would "Implement an environmental infrastructure reconstruction program focused on rebuilding our wastewater" systems.
2024 campaign: Said he would "Streamline the county's Engineering, Public Works and Building departments to increase efficiency" and "speed permitting and cut departmental red tape."
2024 campaign: Said he would "Implement a program of real estate tax credits to encourage affordable, market-based housing development."
2024 campaign: "I will lead the charge to rebuild our environmental infrastructure."
2024 campaign: "We should eliminate sales taxes on the cost of materials for housing, to help make housing more affordable."
2024 campaign: On transit: "we should decrease and limit the use of large buses," shifting toward technology-based, point-to-point service.
2024 campaign: On home rule: "Our cities must be allowed to develop or redevelop as determined by their residents, not by politicians in Tallahassee."
2024 campaign: After the election, wrote on Facebook that "Pinellas County needs rebuilding now and I can't wait to roll up my sleeve and get the job done."
2024 campaign: Did not complete Ballotpedia's 2024 Candidate Connection survey.

electionHistory.text: 2024 general, County Commission District 1: won. Chris Scherer (R) 262,740 (52.98%); Joanne 'Cookie' Kennedy (D) 233,197 (47.02%).
2024 Republican primary, District 1: canceled; Scherer advanced without appearing on the ballot.
Assumed office Nov 19, 2024; current term ends Nov 21, 2028.

keyPositions.text: Voted no on the $312.5 million Rays stadium bond resolution, which passed 5 to 2 on Dec 17, 2024.
Before the Dec 17, 2024 bond vote, pushed for another delay, saying the commission should not vote on bonds until the Rays met all conditions.
On the Rays deal after his election (Nov 2024): "We are in a new era right here," adding that "whatever was agreed to before needs to be looked at differently now."

votes.headline: Changed 2.69 acres on Keystone Road from rural homes to public use
votes.inShort: Sitting as the Countywide Planning Authority, the board changed the countywide land use map for 2.69 acres at 2577 Keystone Road from Residential Rural to Public/Semi-Public, tied to redeveloping an existing community meeting facility there.
votes.officialTitle:
Case No. CW 26-12 - Pinellas County
Countywide Plan Map amendment from Residential Rural and Scenic/Noncommercial Corridor to Public-Semi-Public and Scenic/Noncommercial Corridor, regarding 2.69 acres more or less, located at 2577 Keystone Road.
votes.motion: A motion was made by Commissioner Flowers, seconded by Commissioner Peters, that the item be approved. The motion carried by the following vote:

public.mail: No letters or emails were received.

does.text: Sitting as the Countywide Planning Authority, the board adopted an ordinance changing the countywide land use map for 2.69 acres at 2577 Keystone Road from Residential Rural to Public/Semi-Public. The site already holds a community assembly building, and the change lets the owner replace it with a slightly larger one, with new parking, stormwater work and removal of the current Keystone Road driveway. A companion county zoning overlay limits the site to community assembly with accessory storage; staff listed no fiscal impact.

votes.headline: Funded a $25 million behavioral health urgent care with opioid settlement money
votes.inShort: The county will use opioid settlement money to open an urgent care center for mental health and addiction.
votes.officialTitle: Opioid Abatement Advisory Board's funding recommendation and associated Agreement and Land Use Restriction Agreement with Operation PAR, Inc. for a Behavioral Health Urgent Care Center.

does.text: Approved an agreement of up to $25 million with Operation PAR, Inc. to build and run a walk-in behavioral health urgent care center offering same-day mental health and addiction care, through September 30, 2030. The money comes entirely from regional opioid lawsuit settlement funds held in a separate fund, not the General Fund; staff estimated about $3.4 million for building costs, $2.7 million for start-up and $6.2 million a year for three years of services. A land use restriction requires the property to be used for substance use prevention, treatment or related services through October 1, 2046.

votes.headline: Set the highest tax rates the county can charge next year
votes.inShort: Each summer, Florida counties set a ceiling on next year's property tax rates. Commissioners can lower these rates later but can't go above them. They proposed keeping the countywide rate and 20 other rates unchanged, and raising the Seminole Fire District rate from 1.8000 to 1.9581 mills.

does.text: Set the highest property tax rates the county could adopt for the year starting October 1, 2026; these went on the TRIM notices mailed to owners on August 17. The countywide General Fund rate (4.5423 mills) and 20 other rates stayed at current levels, the Seminole Fire Rescue District ceiling rose from 1.8000 to 1.9581 mills, and the Pinellas Planning Council rate fell from 0.0175 to 0.0171 mills. The board could lower these rates later but not practically raise them.

votes.headline: Raised the trash collection charge for Lealman homes to $288 a year
votes.inShort: Lealman residential property owners pay for county trash pickup through a charge on their tax bill. The board raised it to $288 per home per year.
votes.officialTitle: Annual certificate of the Non-Ad Valorem Assessment Roll and Resolution increasing the Non-Ad Valorem Assessment for the Lealman Solid Waste Collection and Disposal District.
votes.motion: A motion was made by Commissioner Scott, seconded by Commissioner Flowers, that the item be approved. The motion carried by the following vote:

public.mail: Five letters and three voicemails in opposition and one letter in concern have been received.

does.text: Raised the yearly trash collection charge on Lealman residential tax bills from $240 to $288 per home, a $48 increase, and certified the roll so the Tax Collector can bill it. votes.headline: Opted out of a state tax break for some workforce housing
votes.inShort: Florida's Live Local Act lets counties choose whether to give a 75% property tax exemption to rental units for households earning 80% to 120% of area median income. Pinellas chose not to give it.
votes.officialTitle: Resolution electing to not exempt property under Section 196.1978(3)(o), Florida Statutes, commonly known as the Live Local Act Property Tax Exemption.
votes.motion: A motion was made by Vice-Chair Scott, seconded by Commissioner Eggers, that the item be approved. The motion carried by the following vote:

public.mail: No letters or emails were received.

does.text: Chose, for 2025, not to give the optional Live Local Act property tax break on county taxes: a 75% exemption for rental units in complexes of 71 or more units rented to households earning 80% to 120% of area median income. The county could opt out because a Shimberg Center report found a surplus of affordable units for that income range in the Tampa Bay metro area. The required 100% exemption for units serving households at or below 80% of median income was not affected.

after.text: The board renewed the opt-out for 2026 (Resolution 25-138).

votes.headline: Refused to hold a hearing on a dredge permit appeal in Palm Harbor
votes.inShort: Declined a request for a public hearing to appeal a county dredge and fill permit for 106 Harbor Drive. The county attorney said hearing the appeal was up to the board.
votes.officialTitle: Request for a public hearing to appeal the issuance of County Dredge and Fill Permit No. WND-24-00077 for 106 Harbor Drive, Palm Harbor.
votes.motion: A motion was made by Vice-Chair Scott, seconded by Commissioner Flowers, that the item be denied. The motion carried by the following vote:

does.text: Turned down the neighboring owners' (the Myrbacks') request for a public hearing to appeal a county dredge and fill permit issued July 19, 2024, for 106 Harbor Drive in Palm Harbor, which allows dredging of state-owned submerged land around a private dock and boat lift. With no hearing, the permit stands as issued; staff said it was properly issued after the dredge area was reduced to avoid seagrass.

2020 campaign: Said of the 2018 transportation tax: "I supported it when it was on the ballot. I support it now."

electionHistory.text: 2011 general, Tampa City Council District 4: Advanced to runoff (first place). Julie Jenkins 28.94% (4,199); Tony DeSisto 12.33%; Dennis Meyers 7.68%; Joseph V. Citro 6.74%.
2011 runoff, Tampa City Council District 4: Won. Julie Jenkins 39.26% (5,926).
2015 general, Tampa City Council District 4: Won. Kent S. King 28.8% (2,825).
2019 general, Mayor of Tampa: Lost (third place). Jane Castor 48.0% and David Straz 15.5% advanced to the runoff.
2020 Democratic primary, Hillsborough County Commission District 1: Won. Jen McDonald 45.8% (11,785).
2020 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 1: Won. Scott Levinson (R) 49.3% (88,803).
2022 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 1: Won. Scott Levinson (R) 49.6% (57,922). Primaries canceled.
2026 Democratic primary, Hillsborough County Commission District 1: Canceled; advanced without appearing on ballot. Faces Jackie Toledo (R) on Nov 3, 2026.

Jul 16, 2020: As a Hillsborough MPO member he voted yes on the TBX expressway plan in 2016 and later called that vote "complicated".

promises.text: 2024 campaign: Continue to make developers pay their fair share.
2024 campaign: Fight to keep taxes low, budgets balanced, and county spending transparent.
2024 campaign: Work with the Sheriff to keep families safe and fund new initiatives to reduce violent crimes.
2024 campaign: Focus on keeping housing affordable, especially in urban cores.
2024 campaign: Develop new programs and projects that protect the quantity and quality of drinking water.

2022 campaign: In his 2022 race he highlighted opposing a brownfield designation for the former Pebble Creek Country Club, objecting to a yard waste incinerator zoning change in Lutz, backing a New Tampa Performing Arts Center and seeking funds for residential road paving.
2018 campaign: Proposed adding $250,000 to the county budget to speed a potential Kinnan Street connection to Mansfield Boulevard (reported during his 2018 District 2 campaign).

electionHistory.text: 2002 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won (first elected). County page says first elected in 2002. Official 2002 results are not on the SOE results archive, so vote share is not available.

2006 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Kept seat; no District 2 contest appears in the official 2006 primary or general results. Neighborhood News reports he held District 2 from 2002 to 2010. The SOE results do not say whether he was unopposed.
2010 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 5 (countywide): Won. Linda Saul-Sena (DEM) 42.49% (131,504); Jim Hosler (NPA) 4.83% (14,957). No District 5 contest in the 2010 primary results.

2014 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 5 (countywide): Re-elected. Osprey Observer (Dec 17, 2014) calls him re-elected for Countywide District 5. SOE ENR pages soe-2014p and soe-2014g list no District 5 race.
2018 Republican primary, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won. Chris Paradies 27.6% (7,504).
2018 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won. Angela Birdsong (D) 47.6% (67,378).
2022 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won. Angela Birdsong (D) 43.4% (54,444). Republican primary canceled.
2024 Republican primary, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won. Melissa Nordbeck 21.8% (4,188).
2024 general, Hillsborough County Commission District 2: Won. Patricia Altagracia Alonzo (D) 44.9% (74,084). Term ends 2028.

keyPositions.text: Aug 28, 2026: Voted yes on the Development and Funding Agreement, Guaranty and Team Non-Relocation Agreement for a Rays ballpark (RCS 5622; passed 5 to 2).
Aug 28, 2026: Before the Rays vote he said: "To be a world-class community requires vision, courage, bold leadership, and the ability to think big."
May 20, 2026: Voted yes on the non-binding Rays memorandum of understanding (RCS 5486).
Sep 16, 2026: Voted no on a motion to approve the finalized ZooTampa public-private partnership and proceed to a contract (RCS 5654; Cohen, Hagan and Myers voted no).
Sep 24, 2026: Voted yes to adopt FY2027 millage rates (RCS 5671).
Apr 17, 2024: Voted no on enacting the ordinance setting the Community Investment Tax renewal referendum (RCS 4308, Ordinance 24-3; Hagan and Kemp voted no).
Jul 17, 2024: Voted no on approving the School Board's Nov 5, 2024 referendum for additional operating property taxes (RCS 4437; 3 yes, 4 no).
Apr 20, 2022: Voted no on placing the 1 percent transportation surtax ordinance on the Nov 8, 2022 ballot (RCS 3284, Ordinance 22-9).
May 4, 2022: Voted no on the resolution calling the Aug 23, 2022 School Board referendum (RCS 3299).
May 8, 2025: Only no vote on transmitting an Urban Service Area expansion of about 295.6 acres on Lutz Lake Fern Road (RCS 4886).
Sep 18, 2025: Voted yes to adopt FY2026 millage and budget (RCS 5124, 5125; unanimous).
Sep 24, 2026: Roll-call tally (Glass Ballot count of the Clerk PDF, Yes/No/not voting): 2023 476/14/22; 2024 409/17/20; 2025 491/17/37; 2026 through Sep 24: 384/11/13.
Dec 3, 2025: County page calls him the board's leading voice for a Rays ballpark in Ybor City and credits him with creating the Tampa/Hillsborough Film Commission.
Dec 20, 2013: PolitiFact rated Mostly False his Dec 2013 claim that studies suggest the 2017 College Football Playoff championship game would bring about 1,700 to 1,800 full-time jobs.

conflicts.text: Ethics complaint 14-124 resolved by stipulation (final order 14-117) on Article II, Section 8 of the Florida Constitution (financial disclosure).
Florida Politics reports the 2014 complaint led Hagan to pay a $2,000 fine for failing to properly disclose assets on financial disclosure forms.

Aug 2014: the Commission on Ethics agreed to investigate a complaint by George Niemann that Hagan's disclosure listed an investment account ($401,000) and retirement accounts ($219,000) without naming specific assets. Hagan called the complaint "laughable".

A complaint by Niemann and three others alleging free campaign help from consultant Beth Leytham in connection with a Go Hillsborough contract was dismissed by the Commission on Ethics; the Sheriff's Office found no criminal violations in 2016 (as reported).

votes.headline: Approved $75 million for ZooTampa renovations and expansion
votes.inShort: The county will pay ZooTampa $5 million a year through 2041 from Community Investment Tax (half-cent sales tax) money, and the zoo must match it, for $150 million in upgrades and a new South America section. Some commissioners argued the money should be shared with other cultural groups.

does.text: The board approved this package 4 to 3 on Oct 21, 2026, after a public hearing, with Commissioners Cohen, Hagan and Myers voting no; on Oct 7 it had voted 4 to 3 to move toward finalizing the agreement. Approves a 15-year agreement under which the county pays ZooTampa up to $75 million, $5 million a year through 2041, from Community Investment Tax money (a half-cent sales tax), and the zoo matches it one to one, for about $150 million of work. The plan includes upgrades to older habitats, an expanded elephant habitat, a family coaster and a new South America section that extends across North Boulevard onto about 14 acres now used as a City of Tampa maintenance lot. Some commissioners questioned why other eligible groups such as the Children's Museum, Tampa Bay History Center and Straz Center got nothing from this package, while others noted that the same fund sends far more to the Rays stadium, per Bay News 9.

after.text: A majority of the board voted to add ZooTampa capital improvements to the list of projects paid for by the renewed Community Investment Tax. The board also approved an FY 2027 budget amendment putting $5,000,000 in the CIT Extension Project Fund for ZooTampa.

votes.headline: Gave final approval to county funding for a new Rays ballpark
votes.inShort: At a special meeting, the commission approved the development and funding agreement, guaranty and team non-relocation agreement for a Rays ballpark on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus. The county's share is capped at $796 million, and the Rays cover more than $1.3 billion plus cost overruns.

does.text: Approves the Development and Funding Agreement, a guaranty and a team non-relocation agreement for a Rays ballpark and mixed-use district on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus, at Dale Mabry Highway and West Tampa Bay Boulevard. WUSF reported that the county's share is capped at $796 million, including $360 million from the Community Investment Tax (a half-cent sales tax), $263 million backed by the tourist development tax, $103 million in other county funds and $30 million in federal disaster-recovery money (those listed amounts total $756 million; WUSF did not explain the difference), while the Rays pay more than $1.3 billion plus all cost overruns. The county said the Rays plan to open the ballpark in April 2029, and that the board still had to approve a ballpark license and use agreement, a community benefits agreement and a construction funds trust agreement.

after.text: A majority of the board approved an interlocal agreement making the Tampa Sports Authority the county's representative under the Development and Funding Agreement. The authority will oversee design documents, construction materials, schedules and budgets for the stadium.

votes.headline: Approved changes to the proposed FY 2027 budget
votes.inShort: At a budget reconciliation hearing on a recommended $14.1 billion FY 2027 budget, commissioners voted on items they had flagged for change. The plan included a millage swap to support public safety and other county services.

does.text: At the July 29 budget reconciliation hearing, commissioners voted 7 to 0 to approve changes to items they had flagged in the recommended FY 2027 budget, which the county described as a proposed $14.1 billion budget, including a millage swap to support public safety and other services, per a Govly meeting summary. The summary says the board discussed moving money from some nonprofits back to county departments for local infrastructure, but it does not list the individual changes or the tax rates. The vote applied to the recommended budget; the final FY 2027 budget and tax rates were adopted later.

after.text: The county's property tax page, last updated Oct 16, 2026, said the adopted FY 2027 budget cut the countywide property tax rate to 5.3608 mills, down from 5.4608 in FY 2026, and set the unincorporated-area rate at 4.7163 mills. It said about 70% of the adopted unincorporated-area general fund goes to public safety.

votes.inShort: The commission approved a non-binding memorandum of understanding with the Tampa Bay Rays and the City of Tampa for a ballpark and mixed-use district on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus. It set the terms the final contracts would follow.

does.text: Approves a non-binding memorandum of understanding with the Tampa Bay Rays and the City of Tampa for a ballpark and mixed-use district on Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus. It passed 5 to 2 on May 20, 2026. Because it was non-binding, it set the terms for the final contracts but did not commit county money by itself; the final agreements came up for a separate vote in August. WWSB reported a total project cost of about $2.3 billion and a county share in the MOU of up to $796 million ($360 million Community Investment Tax, more than $260 million in tourist tax bonds and $103 million in other county funds).

after.text: The Tampa City Council approved the city's part of the final stadium deal 4 to 3.

promises.text: 2012 campaign: Why running: "We need leaders more concerned about creating jobs than protecting their own."
2012 campaign: Priority on taxes: said it is imperative to stimulate the local economy by reducing taxes on citizens and businesses; said the Penny for Pasco sales tax distributes the burden equally
2012 campaign: Priority on county leadership: called for a nationwide search for a new county administrator with experience in a county of 750,000 to 1,000,000 people
2012 campaign: Priority on mobility fees: said he did not understand replacing impact fees with mobility fees, which he said do not cover the entire cost of infrastructure
2016 campaign: Said the mobility fee formula should change so rural and urban areas pay the same rate; said he did not favor increasing school impact fees
2016 campaign: When filing for the 2016 race, named flooding, redevelopment and transportation as top issues facing the county

electionHistory.text: 2012 Republican primary: Lost County Commission District 1 with 31.29%; Ted Schrader won with 37.49%, Rachel O'Connor 31.22%
2016 Republican primary: Won County Commission District 1, 40.29% over Debbie Wells 32.72% and Rachel O'Connor 26.98%
2016 general: Won County Commission District 1, 69.27% over Dimitri A. Delgado (NPA) 30.35%, with write-in votes
2020: No District 1 contest appears on the Nov 2020 general results page
2024 general: Won County Commission District 1, 59.56% to 40.44% over Lisa Moretti (NPA)
2020: Re-elected to District 1 without a vote after opponent Christopher King withdrew
2024: News report says this is Oakley's third term; first elected in 2016
2012: Spent $176,000 of his own money in the 2012 primary, which he lost to incumbent Ted Schrader; said he did not plan to do so again in 2016

keyPositions.text: Supported an apartment request in Jan 2021: "I think the project fits"
As chairman, voted yes as the board approved an apartment request 3-2 (Apr 2021)
Voted against a gas station land use change, which failed 2-3 (Apr 2021)
Seconded the motion to deny the Seven Oaks apartments, saying the development was too big for the site (Jan 2022)
As chairman, voted for higher school impact fees (2024), citing demand for schools from new residents
Said a proposed solar farm site on Blanton Road with nearby transmission lines seemed suitable, while solar would not work on all farmland (Jun 2018)
As chairman (2024), said most new Pasco homes cost $300,000 to $500,000 and many people moving for jobs cannot afford them

promises.text: 2004 School Board District 4 race: proposed seeking corporate sponsorship to build a Pasco version of Largo's Enterprise Village for elementary students
2004 campaign: Said the district should consider a magnet school or other alternatives for academically advanced children
2004 campaign: Wanted greater environmental awareness in the curriculum, expanding teaching space at the Energy and Marine Center and the SWFWMD facility at Starkey Wilderness Park
2004 campaign: Wanted school green space and athletic fields more accessible to the public

2020 campaign: Said she supports continuing the Penny for Pasco sales tax and defended the current mix of projects it funds; named environmentally sensitive lands preservation, transportation projects and economic development as important areas for future county spending (2020 forum)

electionHistory.text: 2010 Republican primary: Lost State House District 45 in Pasco results, 36.14%, behind Richard Corcoran 45.03%; Fabian Calvo 18.83% (Pasco SOE results page)
2012 Republican primary: Won County Commission District 3 with 43.04% in a five-way race (Chris Gregg 18.39%, Karen King 14.15%, Randy Evans 14.07%, Joshua Josiah Griffin 10.36%)
2012 general: Won County Commission District 3, 58.56% to 41.44% over Matt Murphy (DEM)
2016 Republican primary: Won County Commission District 3, 55.79% to 44.21% over Randy Evans
2016 general: Won County Commission District 3, 62.19% to 37.81% over Barry Horvath (DEM)
2020 general: Won County Commission District 3, 61.29% to 38.71% over Jessica Stempien (DEM)
2024 general: Won County Commission District 3, 89.48% to 10.52% for write-in
2024: News report says this is Starkey's fourth term on the commission; first elected in 2012
School Board: Patch profile lists previous elective office as School Board (2004 and 2008) and an unsuccessful bid in 2010
School Board: campaign site (2012) says she was elected to the School Board in 2004 and served until 2010

keyPositions.text: Said an apartment site was suitable (Jan 2021): "I'm not sure this area is overbuilt for this price point"
Voted yes as the board approved an apartment request 3-2 (Apr 2021); said she wanted evidence the area was oversaturated with apartments
Moved to approve a gas station land use change (Apr 2021); motion failed 2-3
Voted against denial as the board rejected the Seven Oaks apartments (Jan 2022)
Voted for higher school impact fees (2024), saying Pasco's cost of living is "still very affordable" compared with other counties
Said the state Live Local Act benefits institutional investors rather than local developers; met with Senate President Passidomo on it (Jan 2024)
Voted to expand an apartment moratorium area (2022) while saying the county needs more workforce and affordable housing
Voted for the revised Seven Oaks project, approved Nov 2022
Before holding office, led the effort to ban new billboards and founded Scenic Pasco, which lobbied for sign, landscaping and architectural rules (as described in 2004)
Supported a 2019 resolution backing legal hemp cultivation, saying a long wait by the state would put it at a disadvantage
At the Ridge Road extension milestone (Jan 2020), said the road is an important hurricane evacuation route and will add access for the River Ridge school complex

votes.headline: Approved rezoning farmland south of Chancey Road for 96 townhomes
votes.inShort: Changed the zoning on about 20.42 acres in southeast Pasco, south of Chancey Road, from agricultural residential to a planned development that allows 96 townhomes, with conditions.
votes.officialTitle: Zoning Amendment (Regular) - Chanzep LLC - Chanzep MPUD Master Planned Unit Development - A Rezoning Petition Request From an A-R Agricultural Residential District to an MPUD Master Planned Unit Development District to Allow for the Development of 96 Platted Townhome Units and Associated Infrastructure - Southeast Pasco County - Located South of Chancey Road Approximately 777 Feet East of the Chancey Road and Gall Boulevard Intersection - Containing Approximately 20.42 Acres
votes.minutesText: Approved Staff's recommendation with Chairman Mariano voting nay.

does.text: Rezones about 20.42 acres of mostly vacant land south of Chancey Road, east of Gall Boulevard in southeast Pasco, from agricultural-residential to a master planned unit development that allows up to 96 townhomes, about 4.7 homes per acre. The owner, Chanzep LLC, must follow staff's conditions, including landscape buffers along Crystal Springs Road and Chancey Road, a 5-foot sidewalk extension on Crystal Springs Road and a 10-foot multi-use path along Chancey Road. The off-site part of that walking and biking work can be credited against the bike and pedestrian share of the project's mobility fees.

votes.headline: Approved the Two Rivers expansion and a path for a surf park
votes.inShort: Commissioners approved a land use change and rezoning (items P47 and P56) that expand the Two Rivers community in Wesley Chapel and clear the way for a proposed 35-acre surf park. The change adds 900 multifamily homes, of which no more than 240 can be garden-style apartments.

does.text: Expands what can be built in the 3,405-acre Two Rivers development along State Road 56 between Morris Bridge Road and Gall Boulevard in Wesley Chapel. The apartment limit rises from 1,600 to 2,500 units, retail space roughly doubles to about 1.3 million square feet, up to 480 hotel rooms, a 300-bed assisted living facility and one water park of up to 35 acres are added, 209 age-restricted homes are dropped, and the 4,047 single-family homes already allowed stay the same; the board also adopted a matching change to the county's comprehensive plan for Two Rivers. Of the 900 added multifamily homes, no more than 240 may be apartments; the rest must be condos, townhomes, duplexes, villas or similar, per the staff memo. The board changed the condition tying the apartments to the water park at the hearing; Wesley Chapel Community reported the final rule as: the apartments cannot break ground until the surf park gets its certificate of occupancy or three years pass, whichever comes first.

votes.headline: Moved $2 million from county reserves to a New Port Richey septic-to-sewer project
votes.inShort: Transferred $2,000,000 from the county's general fund reserves to the City of New Port Richey to help pay for connecting the Town and Country Villas neighborhood from septic tanks to sewer.
votes.officialTitle: Budget Amendment — Transfer from the Board General Fund Reserves — City of New Port Richey — Funding for Town and Country Villas Septic to Sewer Project — $2,000,000.00
votes.minutesText: Approved Staff's recommendation with Chairman Mariano voting nay.

does.text: Moves $2,000,000 from the county's General Fund reserves and pays it to the City of New Port Richey for the Town and Country Villas neighborhood, where the city plans to replace septic tanks with a sanitary sewer system. The payment carries out a Dec 5, 2023 agreement in which the county pledged $2 million for water and sewer work and the city pledged at least $1.5 million for roads, stormwater, trees and streetlights; the county had budgeted the money in FY 2023, but the agreement terms were not met that year and it was never paid. The city asked for the money after its application for a state Water Quality Improvement Grant for the sewer system was not selected.

votes.headline: Approved $156.2 million in federal disaster recovery money for storm projects
votes.inShort: The board approved $156,162,158.85 in federal disaster recovery (CDBG-DR) money for the first phase of its storm repair and mitigation program after Hurricanes Idalia, Helene and Milton: 22 projects plus $1 million for the county's share of FEMA projects (item R43).

does.text: Approves Phase 1 of Pasco's Better Future Infrastructure and Mitigation Program: 22 projects totaling $155,162,158.85 plus $1,000,000 for the local share of future FEMA repair projects, for $156,162,158.85 in all, paid with federal Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) money for recovery from Hurricanes Idalia, Helene and Milton. Projects include Sea Pines flood abatement in Hudson (about $28.9 million across two line items), Double Hammock Creek flood abatement ($23.9 million), Mitchell Boulevard ($15 million), Elfers septic-to-sewer ($10 million), a Dade City recreation, veterans center and shelter ($12 million) and the Hudson Library renovation. Each project still needs final eligibility, environmental and duplication-of-benefits reviews, procurement and signed agreements before money is committed or construction starts; Bay News 9 reported that projects must be finished within five years or the county may have to repay funds.

after.text: On the consent agenda, the board approved Better Future public services policies and procedures covering $10,000,000 in CDBG-DR funds (item C40, ODRR26-0026).
On the consent agenda, the board approved a budget amendment for Phase 1 Better Future planning projects funded with $7,404,010.20 in CDBG-DR money (item C24, ODRR27-0002).

votes.headline: Renewal of the Sheriff's license-plate camera agreement failed on a 2 to 2 tie
votes.inShort: Commissioner Yeager moved to renew the county's agreement letting the Sheriff's Office run license-plate cameras on county roads. The motion failed 2 to 2, with Commissioner Weightman absent. A tie means a motion fails.

does.text: The motion to keep the county's agreement letting the Pasco Sheriff's Office run license-plate reader cameras on county rights-of-way failed on a 2 to 2 tie: Commissioner Yeager, who made the motion, and Commissioner Starkey voted yes; Commissioner Oakley and Chairman Mariano voted no; Commissioner Weightman was absent. A tie means a motion fails. Because it failed, the renewal was not approved that day; Tampa Bay Beacons reported that the new contract would have switched camera vendors from Flock to Axon. The county agreement covered about 60 cameras in county rights-of-way, while about 110 cameras owned by homeowners associations, stores and other private owners were not part of it, per Tampa Bay Beacons.

after.text: Commissioners discussed a possible committee, a workshop and a task force on license-plate readers. Tampa Bay Beacons reported that the board directed staff to form a task force of residents and experts to study the cameras, drones and related technology, with a public workshop expected before any future program.

Tampa Bay Beacons reported that, the day after the Aug 25 meeting, Sheriff Chris Nocco sent a letter ending the agreement effective Sept 30. Nocco blamed commissioners who no longer supported it and warned that losing the cameras would hurt efforts to solve crimes and find missing people.

votes.headline: Approved pilot programs for school zone speed cameras and safety systems
votes.inShort: Approved two pilot programs: school zone speed detection cameras and the IntelliRoad School Zone Safety System. The item said no county funding was required. The minutes note the Sheriff's deputies will patrol schools as much as they can until the programs start.
votes.officialTitle: Discussion on School Zone Speed Detection Systems (SDS) and IntelliRoad School Zone Safety System (SZSS) Pilot Program – No Funding Required
votes.minutesText: Approved to adopt both programs as per the Sheriff they patrol the schools as much as they can until the program is implemented with Chairman Mariano voting nay.

does.text: Tells county staff to pursue an ordinance allowing school zone speed cameras, and to take part in a no-cost pilot of IntelliRoad's AI-based School Zone Safety System at one school crosswalk. A 2023 state law (HB 657) lets counties ticket drivers going more than 10 mph over a school zone limit. Staff said a Pasco camera program would first need an ordinance, agreements with the Sheriff's Office, New Port Richey and Zephyrhills, a countywide awareness campaign, a vendor and installation, and that ticket money would be split as state law requires among the county, the School District, the state and a crossing guard program. The pilot uses detection cameras, flashing beacons and audio alerts to warn drivers, and staff said this step needs no additional county money.

votes.headline: Put a one-year pause on new data centers
votes.inShort: The county froze permits, rezonings and site plans for new data centers in unincorporated Pasco for 12 months while it works out how to regulate them.

does.text: For 12 months, Pasco County will not accept applications for building permits, site plans, rezonings, comprehensive plan changes or other approvals for data centers and other 'large load' electricity users in unincorporated Pasco. Server or computer rooms that support a site's main use and draw no more than 2.5 megawatts are exempt, and the board can still approve a development agreement for a data center that is not a large load customer if it sets conditions on location, size, water use, power use, noise, electronic waste and other impacts. Tampa Bay Beacons reported that the moratorium is retroactive to May 27, and that planning director David Engel said a proposed data center at Double Branch cannot proceed under it; the pause can end early if the county adopts permanent rules, or the board can extend it by resolution.

promises.text: 2024 campaign: Described himself as "a no-nonsense, rugged individualist with a passion for preserving traditional values and local autonomy"; backs protecting personal liberties, budget discipline and smaller government, guided by a "pragmatic resident-first approach".
2024 campaign: "My main campaign promises were transparency, accountability, putting the residents first, and that's what DOGE is all about" (his own later description of his 2024 campaign promises).

electionHistory.text: 2024 universal primary (all voters), County Commission District 1: Won with 50.3% (15,114 votes). Others: Beth Kirshy Narverud (incumbent) 49.7%. Decided in the primary; no District 1 contest on the Nov 5, 2024 ballot.

keyPositions.text: Nov 19, 2024: Sheriff's Office cyber security funds (Item P-6). Voted no. Return of excess FY 2023-24 cyber security funds and request for FY 2024-25 funds passed 3-2; Amsler and Champion voted no.

Feb 25, 2025: County efficiency committee (local DOGE). Proposed. Presented an ordinance for a Hernando County Department of Government Efficiency. Said: "I'd love to see some bidding on some of our jobs so that we're driving some of the free market there." No vote was reported.

Jan 24, 2026: Flock license plate reader cameras. Proposed an ordinance; objected to installation without board approval. Said: "Government works best when it works in the light." No vote; the board agreed to hold a workshop.
May 8, 2026: Half-cent sales tax referendum for roads. Voted yes (motion failed 3-2). Only Champion and Amsler voted to put the roads surtax on the November ballot.

keyPositions.text: Jan 30, 2019: Firing County Administrator Leonard Sossamon. Voted yes (passed 3-2).

Mar 7, 2023: Impact fee increases (workshop). Supported reviewing fee categories; disagreed that impact fees would hurt growth. On drive-through car washes: "I don't think we're categorizing (drive-through car washes) properly".
Mar 28, 2023: Surplus county property sales (Casey Road, Eagle Drive, Oakhurst Drive). Voted yes (adopted 3-2). Aye: Allocco, Campbell, Hawkins. Nay: Narverud, Champion.

Study of raising school impact fees all at once. Supported (implied by 3-2 count). Said the county is not prepared for the influx of school students and adults seeking homes and recreation (reporter's paraphrase). The article names only Champion and Campbell as no votes.
Nov 19, 2024: Sheriff's Office cyber security funds (Item P-6). Voted yes (passed 3-2).
Mar 3, 2026: Seville West master plan revision. Questioned late-filed documents. Said: "The public is wondering what's going on." The plan passed 3-2; the article does not give individual votes.

May 8, 2026: Half-cent sales tax referendum for roads. Did not support placing it on the ballot (by implication of the 3-2 vote). Said: "If we do nothing, if we don't shift any ad-valorem millage, we're going to get exactly what we have right now."
Jun 2, 2026: Data center moratorium. Supported. Said he is not opposed to data centers but wants guardrails: "If you're not proactive, you're going to get run over."

2024 campaign: "I believe in small government, low taxes and freedom! I support President Trump 100 percent."

2016 general, County Commission District 5: Won with 63.3% (55,892 votes). Others: Paul Douglas (DEM) 36.7%
2020 Republican primary, County Commission District 5: Won with 59.8% (12,271 votes). Others: Kevin Hohn (REP) 40.2%

keyPositions.text: Sep 19, 2017: Lobbyist registration ordinance. Said there was no consensus to bring it forward. Said "there was not a consensus to bring a lobbying ordinance forward" and argued it should not have been placed on the agenda.
Jan 30, 2019: Firing County Administrator Leonard Sossamon. Voted no (passed 3-2). Said: "I think it sets us back. We had a seven-year tenured administrator."

Sep 10, 2019: Second Amendment support letter and resolution. Proposed. Asked the board to send a letter to Gov. DeSantis affirming support for the Second Amendment: "It doesn't change policy ... but it does send a message to Tallahassee." In December 2019 the Tampa Bay Times reported he spearheaded the resolution declaring the county a "Second Amendment sanctuary" (vote count not readable).
Mar 7, 2023: Impact fee increases (workshop). Opposed any increase. Said: "Growth is not guaranteed, and it's not happening right now."
Mar 28, 2023: Surplus county property sales. Voted no (adopted 3-2).
Study of raising school impact fees all at once. Voted no (study approved 3-2). Said he "did not favor a fee increase in the first year without a tax decrease and would vote against it."
Nov 19, 2024: Sheriff's Office cyber security funds (Item P-6). Voted no (passed 3-2).

Jan 24, 2026: Flock license plate reader cameras. Opposed the automated cameras. Said: "This is not an attack on the Sheriff or law enforcement." and "But the Constitution is absolute; it has to be followed."
May 8, 2026: Half-cent sales tax referendum for roads. Voted yes (motion failed 3-2). Said: "We have to do something about the roads."
Sep 21, 2026: FY 2027 Sheriff's Office budget. Supported the sheriff's budget. Thanked Sheriff Al Nienhuis for removing the Flock cameras. His own vote on the 4-1 budget resolution was not reported.

votes.headline: Rejected a second half-cent sales tax vote for roads
votes.inShort: Commissioners voted not to ask voters in November for another half-cent sales tax to fix and maintain roads.

does.text: The proposal would have asked voters in November 2026 to approve a half-cent sales tax to pay only for resurfacing, paving and widening local roads, collected for six years starting January 1, 2027. Because the motion failed 2 to 3 on May 5, 2026 (Amsler and Champion yes; Campbell, Allocco and Hawkins no), the roads tax is not on the ballot. Road work stays funded as before; the county memo says Hernando receives about $12 million a year in gas tax for resurfacing, signals, mowing, potholes and widening.

votes.headline: Approved a $1.76 million amendment to the contract that runs TheBus
votes.inShort: Approved Amendment No. 5 to the county's contract with RATP Dev USA, the company that operates TheBus, for $1,757,078.12, paid for with a federal grant and the 9th-cent gas tax. The motion also put a discussion of bus routes on the first January agenda.
votes.officialTitle: Amendment No. 5 to Contract With RATP Dev USA, Inc., for Transit Operator Services for TheBus (Contract No. 21-RG0010/PH; Amount: $1,757,078.12 Funded by Federal Grant and 9th Cent Gas Tax)
votes.motion: To approve the staff recommendation and place an item on the agenda for the first meeting in January to discuss the bus routes.

does.text: Adds two new TheBus routes (Routes 10 and 11) and paratransit (ADA) service for them, raising the estimated yearly cost of the county's contract with operator RATP Dev USA from $3,443,250.04 to $5,200,328.16, plus a one-time $75,987 startup fee. For FY 2026 it is paid with federal transit grants (FTA 5311 and 5307), a state block grant, and a $947,829 local match moved from 9th-cent gas tax reserves; FY 2027 funding depends on future grants. The motion also put a discussion of bus routes on the first January 2027 agenda.

votes.headline: Committed state housing money to an affordable housing project
votes.inShort: Signed the local government form that commits State Housing Initiative Partnership (SHIP) money to a developer that won Florida Housing Finance Corporation funding for an affordable housing project, on condition of a 50-year affordability period and no tax abatement.

The money comes from federal HOME or state SHIP housing funds, and the form supports the developer's application to Florida Housing Finance Corporation for housing credits. The board added conditions of a 50-year affordability period and no tax abatement.

votes.motion: To deny, and to not bring it back for a second hearing.

votes.inShort: Commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers while staff study how they affect public facilities and draft any needed planning and zoning changes.

does.text: Ordinance No. 2026-15 stops the county from processing development orders and permits for data centers for up to 365 days unless extended or ended early. During the pause, planners are studying effects on water, wastewater, groundwater and the power grid, and plan to bring any needed Comprehensive Plan or zoning changes to the board.

votes.headline: Permanent removal of the CareerSource Polk Executive Director for cause.
votes.officialTitle: Consider the permanent removal of the CareerSource Polk Executive Director for cause.
votes.motion: Motion: 1.) That the Board finds cause pursuant to Section 445.007, Florida Statutes to remove the executive director of CareerSource Polk, Stacy Campbell-Domineck, such cause to include without limitation, neglect of duty, gross mismanagement and lack of performance; and 2:) direct staff to provide Ms. Campbell-Domineck notice of the Board's findings and give her until September 28, 2026, to provide a response to CareerSource Florida's notice and the Compliance and Governance Assessment and why cause does not exist to have her permanently removed; and 3:) place on the October 6, 2026, agenda an item for the Board to consider the permanent removal of Stacy-Campbell Domineck as the executive director of CareerSource Polk; and 4.) Stacy-Campbell Domineck's temporary removal as the executive director of CareerSource Polk shall continue until the temporary removal is terminated by this Board by way of reinstatement or permanent removal by this Board.

statewide.text: On Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, polls are open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time, and anyone in line at 7 p.m. still gets to vote.
Every Florida county offers early voting from October 24 to October 31, and some counties offer extra days.
During early voting you can use any early voting site in the county where you are registered.
On Election Day you must vote at the polling place assigned to your precinct, which is listed on your voter information card and your county elections website.

Bring a current, valid ID that shows your photo and signature, such as a Florida driver license, Florida ID card, U.S. passport, debit or credit card, military ID, student ID, or veteran health ID card.
If your photo ID does not show your signature, bring a second ID that does.
If you do not have an accepted ID with you, you can still vote, but on a provisional ballot.
A picture of your ID on your phone does not count, so bring the actual card.
statewide.publisher: Hillsborough County Supervisor of Elections (2026 Voter Guide)

statewide.text: If you believe you are registered but your name cannot be found at your polling place, ask for a provisional ballot.
After voting a provisional ballot, you have until 5 p.m. on the second day after the election (Thursday, November 5) to give your Supervisor of Elections written proof that you are eligible.
A provisional ballot counts if you are eligible, you voted in the right precinct, and your signature matches the one on your voter record.
A mail ballot counts only if it reaches your county Supervisor of Elections by 7 p.m. on Election Day, and a postmark does not count.
The deadline to have a mail ballot sent to you was Thursday, October 22, 2026, so it is now too late to request one by mail.

You can still pick up your own mail ballot at your Supervisor of Elections office, but now that early voting has started you must sign a form saying an emergency keeps you from voting early or at your polling place.
If you asked for a mail ballot but would rather vote in person, bring the mail ballot with you, filled in or not.
You may bring a sample ballot or your own notes into the voting booth to help you remember your choices.
statewide.publisher: Hillsborough County Supervisor of Elections (Oct 22, 2026 release)

statewide.text: First time voting? It is okay to skip races, and if you make a mistake on your ballot, ask for a new one instead of crossing it out.
statewide.publisher: Hillsborough County Supervisor of Elections (2026 Voter Guide)

pinellas.earlyVoting: Early voting runs October 19 through November 1; the county calendar lists it from 7 a.m. October 19 to 7 p.m. November 1, so check VotePinellas.gov for each site's daily hours.
pinellas.mailBallotDropOff: Return your mail ballot to a Supervisor of Elections office or one of the secure ballot return locations listed at VotePinellas.gov so it arrives by 7 p.m. on November 3.

hillsborough.earlyVoting: Early voting runs every day from October 19 through November 1, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., at any of 27 sites.
hillsborough.mailBallotDropOff: Drop your mail ballot in the secure ballot intake station inside any early voting site during early voting hours, or at a Supervisor of Elections office when it is open, so it arrives by 7 p.m. on November 3; polling places cannot accept it.

pasco.earlyVoting: Early voting runs every day from Monday, October 19 through Saturday, October 31, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
pasco.mailBallotDropOff: Mail your ballot or drop it at any Pasco early voting site or one of the three Supervisor of Elections offices so it arrives by 7 p.m. on November 3; polling places cannot accept it.

hernando.earlyVoting: Early voting runs every day from Thursday, October 22 through Saturday, October 31, 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., at five sites.
hernando.mailBallotDropOff: Drop your mail ballot at the secure ballot intake station at the Brooksville main office (weekdays 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.), the Forest Oaks office in Spring Hill, or any early voting site during early voting hours, so it arrives by 7 p.m. on November 3.

county-commission.oneLine: Passes county laws, approves the county budget, sets property tax rates, and directly governs areas outside city limits, including zoning decisions.

school-board.oneLine: Runs the county's public schools: sets school policies, adopts the school budget and school tax rate, approves building plans, and assigns students to schools.

unconfirmed: Pinellas early voting daily hours: the SOE calendar shows only '7:00 AM Oct 19 to 7:00 PM Nov 1' as one range. FOX 13 reports 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily, but no fetched official page states daily hours or the site list.
Pinellas 2026 general election secure ballot return locations and hours: the SOE says they are listed on its election page, but the list itself (a PDF or page) could not be found or loaded.
Pasco number and list of 2026 general early voting sites: not shown on the fetched schedule page.
Hillsborough sample ballot deep link: the SOE says to look it up at VoteHillsborough.gov; the lookup tool's exact URL was not visible in fetched pages.

Notes or sample ballot in the booth: no Florida Division of Elections page fetched says this. The source is Hillsborough SOE (Oct 22, 2026). Pasco SOE says to bring a marked sample ballot to the polling place. Hernando SOE said the same in a 2014 sample ballot.

Precinct rule and provisional-counting rule come from a 2024 Florida DOS Election Day press release; the 2026 version was not found. The precinct rule is also stated by Hillsborough SOE (Oct 16, 2026) and Hernando SOE (Ways to Vote page).

The main Division of Elections Election Day and vote-by-mail pages (dos.fl.gov/elections/for-voters/voting/election-day-voting/ and .../vote-by-mail/) would not load, so the ID and provisional ballot facts cite the Florida Statutes on flsenate.gov.
No first-time voter tip from the Division of Elections was found; the tip used is from Hillsborough SOE's 2026 Voter Guide.
